source.title: Concept Heterogeneity-aware Representation Steering
source.authors: Laziz U. Abdullaev; Noelle Y. L. Wong; Ryan Lee; Shi-Qi Jiang; Khoi Nguyen; T. Nguyen

record.file_problem: The provided text includes the paper and its supplement through Appendix E.7; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares single global difference-in-means steering with cluster-dependent steering and reports jailbreak results. This refines the single-direction account, although the per-model results for the standard Directional Ablation baseline are not reliably assignable from the flattened table.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates jailbreaking with activation addition and Directional Ablation, and separately varies the number of clusters. These outcomes bear on jailbreak behavior and heterogeneous steering. The toxicity-mitigation and image-style experiments do not test refusal behavior. Per-model ASR cells for standard Directional Ablation in Table 2 are not reliably assignable from the flattened extraction, so they are not recorded as individual results.
record.test_reason: The study re-runs Arditi-style difference-in-means Directional Ablation and ActAdd jailbreaks on seven instruct models. It reports ASR and tinyBenchmarks utility for each, then shows that an input-dependent, multi-cluster steering field (CHaRS) beats the single global direction. That bears on V1 (the DiM baseline numbers) and on V4 (whether more than one direction helps). Contrary to the record, Tables 1 and 2 are readable: ASR values appear in model order for the ActAdd, CHaRS and CHaRS-PCT rows.
record.authors_conclusion: The first sentence is right. The authors argue that concepts are represented heterogeneously (clustered) and that single global difference-in-means steering is brittle. Their input-dependent OT/GMM steering (CHaRS) consistently outperforms ActAdd and DirAbl in ASR while preserving utility. The record's claim that they call the work 'a refinement, not a direct test' of single-direction ablation is the reader's inference, not the authors' statement.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of relying solely on one global difference-in-means vector, CHaRS clusters source and target activations and uses an optimal-transport plan to construct input-dependent steering vectors. For jailbreak experiments, it uses last-token activations to construct candidate directions and selects an intervention layer.
record.method_sensitivity: Cluster count affects jailbreak ASR, with no clear general trend and tuning reported as potentially necessary.

fits_no_version.finding: CHaRS beats Linear-AcT in toxicity mitigation and in FLUX.1 image-style steering.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Heterogeneity-aware steering generalizes beyond refusal (not a refusal-direction claim).

fits_no_version.finding: k-means on last-token activations of harmful prompts yields semantically coherent harm categories (Table 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful-instruction representations are clustered by harm type.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The standard Directional Ablation ASR values in Table 2 are not reliably assignable from the flattened table extraction. The text reports a maximum relative gain without giving absolute ASR values for that comparison. The study does not test the all-layers-and-positions intervention or the harmless-request addition part of V1.
record.rows_left_out: Per-model standard Directional Ablation ASR cells and associated tinyBenchmark cells from Table 2 were not extracted because the flattened table layout does not reliably align the values with model and method. Other task results (toxicity mitigation and image style control) do not measure refusal behavior.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; the effect of ablation on refusal of harmless prompts; ASR with no steering (blank in tables).
All: no weight edit or released abliterated models.
All: no prompt-based jailbreak analysis and no training against ablation; the 'jailbreak' here is the steering itself.

missing.what: Per-model DiM DirAbl ASR: Gemma 79.81, Llama3.1-8B 91.35, Llama3.2-3B 83.65, Qwen3B 90.38, Qwen7B 89.42, Qwen14B 78.85, Qwen32B 82.69; plus CHaRS/CHaRS-PCT values
tinyBenchmarks averages under DirAbl vs no steering (utility largely preserved)
Per-model DiM ActAdd vs CHaRS ASR (e.g. Llama3.2-3B 74.04→79.81; Qwen32B 82.69→89.42) and the large utility drop under ActAdd (Gemma avg 71.11→51.39)
CHaRS-PCT below DiM baseline for some PC counts; diagonal-covariance variant worse than equal covariance; coupling strategy (uniform coupling best 87.50 < DiM 91.35)
K sweep under DirAbl for Qwen3B (best K=11) and Gemma (best K=9)

record.verdict_notes: The record wrongly says Table 2 cells are unassignable. Values read in order (DiM baseline, CHaRS, CHaRS-PCT; the No Steering ASR is blank) and match the prose ('up to 5%' = Gemma 79.81→84.62; 'up to 7%' ActAdd = Gemma and Qwen32B). ActAdd here adds the harmful→harmless shift to harmful prompts, so it does not test the 'adding induces refusal' part of V1. The evaluation set is 104 prompts, so one prompt ≈ 0.96 ASR points. No significance tests or seeds for the ASR results. Peer reviewed (ICML 2026).

versions.untested_parts: The study applies selected-layer Directional Ablation and evaluates jailbreak ASR, but the standard Directional Ablation ASR cells could not be reliably assigned to models from the flattened Table 2. It does not test ablation at every layer and position, whether all refusals disappear, general capability under that exact intervention, or adding the direction to harmless requests.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.

The paper evaluates jailbreak steering with Directional Ablation, but its baseline per-model ASR results could not be reliably assigned from the flattened Table 2. It does not train models against ablation or test resulting robustness.

The study compares global difference-in-means steering with cluster-dependent steering on jailbreak ASR. It does not establish whether refusal is represented specifically as an affine structure, a cone, or a dominant direction plus others.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No transfer test across languages, base-to-instruct models, or model variants of the direction.
No comparison of refusal-training procedures or timing.
No reasoning-model test of the single-direction claim.

relation.reason: The study reports DiM ablation ASR and utility, plus the ASR from multi-direction ablation, on its own runs (Tables 1–2, Figs 5, 8–11, Table 10).

tranche.reason: The authors argue that a single global DiM direction assumes homogeneity and is brittle. They rerun Arditi-style DiM DirAbl/ActAdd on 7 models and show that input-dependent multi-cluster directions raise ASR, which is evidence that the single-direction version needs restating.

source_check.notes: The No Steering rows in Tables 1–2 give no ASR, and K/PC counts were tuned on the 104-prompt eval split. The DiM layer-selection method and the CHaRS steering strength α are not stated. Missing items: Table 2 rows for V1. DiM ActAdd (harmful→harmless) cuts tinyBenchmark averages by 5–20 points (Gemma 71.11→51.39, Table 1).

statements.correction: CHaRS > DiM in all 14 model×intervention cells: ActAdd +0.96 to +6.73 points, DirAbl +0.96 to +4.81 points (Tables 1–2; 104 eval prompts). CHaRS-PCT < DiM in Table 1 for Qwen2.5-14B ActAdd (93.27 vs 94.23). K and PC count were chosen by best ASR on the same eval split (App. E.4–E.5).
statements.problem: No factual error. The 104 prompts, the 0.96-point one-prompt gains (Qwen14B ActAdd, Llama8B DirAbl, Qwen7B DirAbl), the lack of a clear K trend, and CHaRS-PCT falling below DiM for some PC counts (Fig 11, Qwen3B DirAbl) are all in the text. Context is missing: CHaRS beat DiM in every cell, and the one-prompt gains are not in the cited rows R1/R2.
